text: The Deepwater Horizon oil spill began on 20 April 2010 off the coast of the United States in the Gulf of Mexico, at the BP-operated Macondo Prospect in Mississippi Canyon Block 253, approximately 41 mi (66 km) off the Louisiana coast. The disaster started when high-pressure methane gas expanded into the marine riser and ignited at approximately 7:45 p.m. CDT, causing an explosion that engulfed the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig, resulting in the deaths of eleven crew members who were never found, and the rescue of ninety-four others, seventeen of whom were injured. The rig sank on 22 April 2010. An oil slick was discovered the same day, and oil flowed for 87 days. The United States federal government estimated the total discharge at 4.9 million barrels (210,000,000 US gal; 780,000 m³), with a plus-or-minus 10% uncertainty, making it the largest marine oil spill in petroleum industry history and 8 to 31 percent larger than the Ixtoc I spill. BP initially estimated a flow rate of 1,000 to 5,000 barrels per day, but the Flow Rate Technical Group estimated an initial rate of 62,000 bbl/d (9,900 m³/d). The spill directly affected 70,000 sq mi (180,000 km²) of ocean, comparable to the area of Oklahoma, with oil washing up on 125 mi (201 km) of Louisiana’s coast and along the Mississippi, Florida, and Alabama coastlines by early June 2010. Oil reached Gulf Park Estates in Mississippi in late June, Grand Isle and Lake Pontchartrain in July, and a new wave of oil coated 16 mi (26 km) of Louisiana coastline in September. By October, weathered oil reached Texas. As of July 2011, about 491 mi (790 km) of coastline in Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida were contaminated, with a total of 1,074 mi (1,728 km) oiled since the spill began. By December 2012, 339 mi (546 km) of coastline remained subject to evaluation and cleanup. The spill affected marine and wildlife habitats, fishing, and tourism industries, with oil found as far as the Florida Panhandle and Tampa Bay, where dispersant-treated oil was embedded in sand. In April 2013, dolphins and other marine life continued to die in record numbers, with infant dolphins dying at six times the normal rate. Studies in 2014 found that tuna and amberjack exposed to the oil developed heart and organ deformities, and cardiotoxicity was widespread in exposed animal life. Investigations attributed the explosion to defective cement on the well, primarily blaming BP, but also Transocean and Halliburton, with a White House commission concluding the spill resulted from "systemic" root causes and warning of recurrence without reform. In November 2012, BP pleaded guilty to 11 counts of manslaughter, two misdemeanors, and a felony count of lying to Congress, agreed to four years of government monitoring, and was temporarily banned from new U.S. government contracts, paying $4.525 billion in fines and other payments. As of 2018, cleanup costs, charges, and penalties exceeded $65 billion. In September 2014, a U.S. District Court judge ruled BP was primarily responsible due to gross negligence and reckless conduct. In April 2016, BP agreed to pay $20.8 billion in fines, the largest environmental damage settlement in U.S. history. The Deepwater Horizon was a 10-year-old semi-submersible drilling rig built by Hyundai Heavy Industries, owned by Transocean, and operated under the Marshallese flag, chartered to BP from March 2008 to September 2013. It was drilling a deep exploratory well 18,360 ft (5,600 m) below sea level in approximately 5,100 ft (1,600 m) of water. BP held a 65% share of the Macondo Prospect, with 25% owned by Anadarko Petroleum and 10% by MOEX Offshore 2007, a unit of Mitsui. BP attempted to cap the well using remotely operated vehicles, a containment dome, and a "top kill" method, all of which failed. A riser insertion tube and stopper were used to divert oil, collecting 924,000 US gal (22,000 bbl; 3,500 m³) before being removed. A second containment system was connected to the blowout preventer on 16 June 2010, and a better-fitting cap ("Top Hat Number 10") was installed on 10 July. A final device with a larger chamber and manual valve was secured on 15 July 2010, sealing the well. Relief wells were drilled starting in May 2010, with the first test oil and mud pumped on 3 August 2010, and cement pumped into the well on 4 August 2010. The failed blowout preventer was removed on 3 September 2010, and a replacement was installed. Cement pumping began on 16 September 2010, and the well was declared sealed on 19 September 2010. Despite this, reports in early 2012 indicated the well site was still leaking. Oil slicks were reported in March 2011, August 2011, March 2012, October 2012, and January 2013, with chemical analysis confirming the oil originated from the Macondo well. The U.S. Coast Guard initially claimed the oil was too dispersed to recover, but later warned BP and Transocean of financial liability. A white, milky substance was observed seeping from the wreckage, which BP and the U.S. Coast Guard stated was not oil and not harmful. In October 2012, BP reported plugging a leak from a failed containment dome. In December 2012, a U.S. Coast Guard subsea survey found no oil from the wells or wreckage, though the source of the oil sheen remained unknown. Scientists suggested the sheen could be residual oil or formation oil escaping through a subsurface fault, potentially indicating an indefinite release. The fundamental strategies were containment, dispersal, and removal, with approximately 47,000 people and 7,000 vessels involved in summer 2010. By 3 October 2012, federal response costs reached $850 million, mostly reimbursed by BP. By January 2013, 935 personnel remained involved, and cleanup had cost BP over $14 billion. The total estimated volume of leaked oil was 4.9 million barrels (780,000 m³), with BP arguing that government figures did not account for over 810,000 bbl (34 million US gal; 129,000 m³) of oil collected or burned before reaching the Gulf. The spill also released thousands of tons of hydrocarbon gases into the atmosphere. Researchers found deep plumes of dissolved oil and gas remained confined to the northern Gulf, with long-lasting impacts on dissolved oxygen. Estimates suggested up to 75% of the oil remained below the surface, with over 100×10⁶ US gal (2.4 million barrels) remaining in the Gulf. In 2013, over 4,600,000 lb (2,100 t) of oily material was removed from Louisiana’s coast, and tar balls continued to wash up on Alabama and Florida Panhandle beaches. Cleanup patrols were reduced to an as-needed basis, and scientists at the Gulf of Mexico Oil Spill and Ecosystem Science Conference suggested up to one-third of the oil may have mixed with deep ocean sediments, risking damage to ecosystems and fisheries. A 2013 study found a dispersant-treated oil plume had reached 80 mi (130 km) off the Tampa Bay region, with possible fish lesions.

Well casing acted as a flow conduit, possibly intersecting a naturally occurring fault, and then escaping at the surface some distance from the wellhead. If the substance released was oil from the subsurface, it could indicate an indefinite release of oil. The oil slick was comparable in size to naturally occurring oil seeps and was not large enough to pose an immediate threat to wildlife. The fundamental strategies for addressing the spill were containment, dispersal, and removal. In summer 2010, approximately 47,000 people and 7,000 vessels were involved in the response. By 3 October 2012, federal response costs reached $850 million, mostly reimbursed by BP. As of January 2013, 935 personnel were still involved, and by that time, cleanup had cost BP over $14 billion. It was estimated with plus-or-minus 10% uncertainty that 4.9 million barrels (780,000 m³) of oil was released from the well; 4.1 million barrels (650,000 m³) went into the Gulf. A report by the Department of the Interior and NOAA stated that "75% [of oil] has been cleaned up by Man or Mother Nature"; however, only about 25% of released oil was collected or removed, while about 75% remained in the environment in one form or another. In 2012, Markus Huettel, a benthic ecologist at Florida State University, maintained that while much of BP's oil was degraded or evaporated, at least 60% remains unaccounted for. In May 2010, a local native set up a network for people to volunteer in cleaning up beaches, offering boat use through the Vessels of Opportunity program; however, only a third of registered boats participated, leading to disappointment and prompting the formation of The Florida Key Environmental Coalition, which gained significant influence in the clean-up efforts. Containment booms stretching over 4,200,000 ft (1,300 km) were deployed, either to corral oil or protect ecologically sensitive areas like marshes, mangroves, shrimp/crab/oyster ranches; booms extend 18–48 in (0.46–1.22 m) above and below the water surface and were effective only in calm, slow-moving waters. Including one-time use sorbent booms, a total of 13,300,000 ft (4,100 km) of booms were deployed. Booms were criticized for washing up on shore, allowing oil to escape above or below, and being ineffective in waves over three to four feet (90–120 cm). The Louisiana barrier island plan was developed to protect Louisiana's coast but was criticized for expense and poor results, with critics alleging it was politically motivated with little scientific input. The EPA expressed concern that booms threatened wildlife. A group called Matter of Trust campaigned to encourage hair salons, dog groomers, and sheep farmers to donate hair, fur, and wool clippings stuffed in pantyhose or tights to contain oil near shores, a technique from the Exxon Valdez disaster. The spill was notable for the volume of Corexit oil dispersant used and for experimental application methods. Altogether, 1.84×10⁶ US gal (7,000 m³) of dispersants were used; 771,000 US gal (2,920 m³) were released at the wellhead. Subsea injection, never previously tried, was used due to the spill's unprecedented nature, with BP, USCG, and EPA jointly deciding on it. Over 400 sorties were flown to release the product. Although dispersant use was described as "the most effective and fast moving tool for minimizing shoreline impact," the approach continues to be investigated. A 2011 analysis by Earthjustice and Toxipedia showed the dispersant contained cancer-causing agents, hazardous toxins, and endocrine-disrupting chemicals. Environmental scientists expressed concerns that dispersants increased toxicity to sea turtles and bluefin tuna, especially when applied at the source, as they are carried by currents through the Gulf. According to BP and federal officials, dispersant use stopped after the cap was in place; however, marine toxicologist Riki Ott wrote in an open letter to the EPA that Corexit use continued after that date, and a GAP investigation stated that "a majority of GAP witnesses cited indications that Corexit was used after [July 2010]." A NALCO manual obtained by GAP stated that Corexit 9527 is an "eye and skin irritant" and may cause hemolysis, kidney or liver injury, central nervous system effects, nausea, vomiting, anesthetic or narcotic effects, advising not to get it in eyes, on skin, or on clothing, and to wear protective clothing. For Corexit 9500, the manual advised the same precautions and to avoid breathing vapor. According to FOIA requests, neither protective gear nor the manual were distributed to Gulf cleanup workers. Corexit EC9500A and EC9527A were the principal variants. These formulations are neither the least toxic nor the most effective among EPA-approved dispersants, but BP chose them because they were available the week of the rig explosion. On 19 May, the EPA gave BP 24 hours to choose less toxic alternatives from the National Contingency Plan Product Schedule and begin applying them within 72 hours of approval or provide a detailed reason why no approved products met the standards. On 20 May, BP determined that none of the alternative products met all three criteria of availability, non-toxicity, and effectiveness. On 24 May, EPA Administrator Lisa P. Jackson ordered EPA to evaluate alternatives and ordered BP to reduce dispersant use by 75%. BP reduced Corexit use from 25,689 to 23,250 US gal (97,240 to 88,010 L) per day, a 9% decline. On 2 August 2010, the EPA stated that dispersants did no more harm to the environment than the oil and that they stopped a large amount of oil from reaching the coast by breaking it down faster. However, some independent scientists and EPA experts continue to voice concerns. Underwater injection of Corexit into the leak may have created oil plumes discovered below the surface. Because the dispersants were applied at depth, much of the oil never rose to the surface. One plume was 22 mi (35 km) long, more than 1 mi (1,600 m) wide, and 650 ft (200 m) deep. Experts were most concerned about the slow breakdown of oil in cold, 40°F (4°C) water at depths of 3,000 ft (900 m). In late 2012, a study from Georgia Tech and Universidad Autonoma de Aguascalientes in Environmental Pollution reported that Corexit used during the BP oil spill increased the toxicity of the oil by 52 times. The scientists concluded that "mixing oil with dispersant increased toxicity to ecosystems" and made the Gulf oil spill worse. The three basic approaches for removing oil from water were combustion, offshore filtration, and collection for later processing. USCG reported recovering 33,000,000 US gal (120,000 m³) of tainted water, including 5,000,000 US gal (19,000 m³) of oil. BP reported recovering or flaring 826,800 bbl (131,450 m³). It is calculated that about 5% of leaked oil was burned at the surface and 3% was skimmed. On the most demanding day, 47,849 people were assigned and over 6,000 marine vessels, 82 helicopters, and 20 fixed-wing aircraft were involved. From April to mid-July 2010, 411 controlled in-situ fires remediated approximately 265,000 bbl (11.1 million US gal; 42,100 m³). The fires released small amounts of toxins, including cancer-causing dioxins. According to EPA's report, the released amount is not enough to pose an added cancer risk to workers and coastal residents, while a second research team concluded only a small added risk. Oil was collected using skimmers; in total, 2,063 various skimmers were used. For offshore, more than 60 open-water skimmers were deployed, including 12 purpose-built vehicles. EPA regulations prohibited skimmers that left more than 15 parts per million (ppm) of oil in the water. Many large-scale skimmers exceeded the limit. Due to Corexit use, the oil was too dispersed to collect, according to a spokesperson for shipowner TMT. In mid-June 2010, BP ordered 32 machines that separate oil and water, each capable of extracting up to 2,000 bbl/d (320 m³/d). After one week of testing, BP began proceeding, and by 28 June, had removed 890,000 bbl (141,000 m³). After the well was capped, shore cleanup became the main task. Two main types of affected coast were sandy beaches and marshes. On beaches, techniques included sifting sand, removing tar balls, and digging out tar mats manually or mechanically. For marshes, techniques such as vacuum and pumping, low-pressure flush, vegetation cutting, and bioremediation were used. Dispersants are said to facilitate microbial digestion of oil, but conflicting results have been reported. Mixing dispersants with oil at the wellhead would keep some oil below the surface, allowing microbes to digest it before it reached the surface. Risks included increased microbial activity reducing subsea oxygen levels, threatening fish and other animals. Several studies suggest microbes successfully consumed part of the oil. By mid-September, other research claimed microbes mainly digested natural gas rather than oil. David L. Valentine, a professor of microbial geochemistry at UC Santa Barbara, said the capability of microbes to break down the leaked oil had been greatly exaggerated. However, biogeochemist Chris Reddy said natural microorganisms were a major reason the oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico was not far worse. Genetically modified Alcanivorax borkumensis was added to waters to speed digestion. The delivery method of microbes to oil patches was proposed by the Russian Research and Development Institute of Ecology and the Sustainable Use of Natural Resources. On 18 May 2010, BP was designated the lead "Responsible Party" under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, granting operational authority to coordinate the response. The first video images were released on 12 May, and further images were released by members of Congress who had access through BP. During the spill response, at the request of the Coast Guard, the FAA implemented a 900 sq mi (2,300 km²) temporary flight restriction zone over the operations area to prevent civilian air traffic from interfering with response aircraft. All flights in the area were prohibited except those authorized by air traffic control, routine flights supporting offshore oil operations, federal, state, local, and military flights supporting response, and air ambulance and law enforcement operations. Exceptions were granted on a case-by-case basis based on safety, operational requirements, weather, and traffic volume. No flights, except those conducting aerial chemical dispersing operations or for landing and takeoff, were allowed below 1,000 m (3,300 ft). Despite restrictions, there were 800 to 1,000 flights per day. Local and federal authorities, citing BP's authority, denied press access to document the spill from the air, boats, or on the ground, blocking access to public areas. In some cases, photographers were granted access only with BP officials escorting them on BP-contracted boats and aircraft. In one example, the U.S. Coast Guard stopped Jean-Michel Cousteau's boat and allowed it to proceed only after being assured no journalists were on board. In another, a CBS News crew was denied access to oil-covered beaches and told, "This is BP's rules, not ours." Some members of Congress criticized the restrictions on journalist access. The FAA denied that BP employees or contractors made decisions on flights or access, stating those decisions were made by the FAA and Coast Guard. The FAA acknowledged that media access was limited to hired planes or helicopters, arranged through the Coast Guard. The Coast Guard and BP denied having a policy of restricting journalists, noting that media had been embedded with authorities since the beginning, with over 400 embeds aboard boats and aircraft, and that they wanted to provide access while maintaining safety. On 15 April 2014, BP announced that coastal cleanup was substantially complete, while the U.S. Coast Guard continued using physical barriers such as floating booms to prevent further spread. Skimmer boats removed a majority of the oil and sorbents absorbed any remnant oil like a sponge. Although the method did not remove oil completely, chemicals called dispersants were used to hasten oil degradation to prevent further damage to marine habitats below the surface. For the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, cleanup workers used 1,400,000 US gal (5,300,000 L; 1,200,000 imp gal) of various chemical dispersants. The state of Louisiana received funding from BP to conduct regular testing of fish, shellfish, water, and sand. Initial testing regularly showed detectable levels of dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, a chemical used in cleanup. Testing over 2019 reported by GulfSource.org showed no results for the pollutants tested. Due to the Deepwater Horizon spill, marine life was suffering, with thousands of animals visibly covered in oil. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, working with the Smithsonian's National Zoological Park, rescued animals to assist in cleanup, although many animals were found dead. The spill area hosts 8,332 species, including more than 1,270 fish, 604 polychaetes, 218 birds, 1,456 mollusks, 1,503 crustaceans, 4 sea turtles, and 29 marine mammals. Between May and June 2010, the spill waters contained 40 times more polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.

The Deepwater Horizon spill caused widespread environmental and health impacts. The state of Louisiana received funding from BP to conduct regular testing of fish, shellfish, water, and sand, though initial tests detected dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, a cleanup chemical, and later testing over 2019 by GulfSource.org reported no results. Marine life suffered significantly, with thousands of animals visibly covered in oil, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, in collaboration with the Smithsonian's National Zoological Park, rescued animals while many were found dead. The spill area hosts 8,332 species, including over 1,270 fish, 604 polychaetes, 218 birds, 1,456 mollusks, 1,503 crustaceans, 4 sea turtles, and 29 marine mammals. Between May and June 2010, spill waters contained 40 times more polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) than before the spill, with PAHs most concentrated near the Louisiana Coast and levels increasing 2–3 fold off Alabama, Mississippi, and Florida. PAHs are carcinogenic and pose health risks to humans and marine life, and they can harm marine species directly while microbes used to break down oil may reduce oxygen levels. The oil contained approximately 40% methane by weight, compared to about 5% in typical oil deposits, which can suffocate marine life and create "dead zones." A 2014 study funded by NOAA, Stanford University, and the Monterey Bay Aquarium and published in Science found that oil toxins caused irregular heartbeats and cardiac arrest, with PAH cardiotoxicity potentially affecting many species. Another peer-reviewed study from 2014, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that tuna and amberjack exposed to spill oil developed fatal or life-shortening heart and organ deformities, with scientists suggesting these effects could apply to other large predator fish and humans due to similar developing hearts. BP claimed the oil concentrations in the study were rarely seen in the Gulf, but The New York Times reported this contradicted the study. The oil dispersant Corexit, previously used only on the surface, was released underwater in unprecedented amounts to make oil more biodegradable, emulsifying it into tiny droplets that remained suspended in water and on the sea floor. The oil and dispersant mixture entered the food chain via zooplankton, with signs of the mix found under the shells of blue crab larvae, and insect populations in coastal marshes were significantly impacted. Petroleum compounds and Corexit were found in migratory bird eggs as far as Minnesota. Dispersant and PAHs were believed to cause "disturbing numbers" of mutated fish, including 50% of shrimp lacking eyes and eye sockets, and fish with sores and lesions were first noted by fishermen in November 2010; prior to the spill, about 0.1% of Gulf fish had lesions, but estimates rose to 20% and later 50%. In October 2013, Al Jazeera reported the Gulf ecosystem was "in crisis" due to declining seafood catches, deformities, and lesions. Researchers J. Christopher Haney, Harold Geiger, and Jeffrey Short concluded that over one million coastal birds died directly from the spill, supported by National Audubon Society observations of bird mortality after the acute phase. In July 2010, the spill was reported to be having a "devastating" effect on marine life, with damage to the ocean floor endangering the Louisiana pancake batfish, whose range is entirely within the spill area. A definitive link between the spill and the death of a Gulf coral community was found in March 2012. NOAA has recognized a cetacean Unusual Mortality Event (UME) since before the spill and is investigating possible connections to the spill, with potential criminal charges if a link is established; only 2% of killed mammal carcasses have been recovered. In the first birthing season after the spill, dead baby dolphins were found at about 10 times the normal number along Mississippi and Alabama shorelines. A NOAA/BP study found nearly half the bottlenose dolphins tested in mid-2011 in Barataria Bay were in "guarded or worse" condition, including 17% not expected to survive. BP denies the disease conditions are related to the spill, stating dolphin deaths began before the spill. By 2013, over 650 dolphins had been stranded, a four-fold increase over the historical average. The National Wildlife Federation reports that sea turtle strandings, mostly of endangered Kemp's ridley sea turtles, increased from an average of 100 per year before the spill to roughly 500 since the spill. NWF senior scientist Doug Inkley noted the marine death rates were unprecedented and occurring high in the food chain, suggesting "something amiss" with the Gulf ecosystem. In December 2013, a study in Environmental Science & Technology found half of 32 dolphins captured near southeastern Louisiana were seriously ill or dying. BP called the report "inconclusive" regarding spill causation. Tar balls continued to wash up along the Gulf coast in 2012 and were still found in Mississippi and Louisiana coasts in 2013, along with oil sheens in marshes and severe coastal erosion due to tree and marsh grass death. In 2013, former NASA physicist Bonny Schumaker noted a "dearth of marine life" within 30 to 50 miles of the well after multiple flights since May 2010. In 2013, researchers found oil on the seafloor was not degrading and observed a "dirty blizzard" where oily particles clumped around sediments and fell to the ocean floor, potentially having long-term effects as oil could remain in the food chain for generations. A 2014 bluefin tuna study found that oil broken down by wave action and dispersants was more toxic than fresh oil. A 2015 study found that dispersants were more toxic than oil to coral. A 2015 NOAA study published in PLOS ONE linked the sharp increase in dolphin deaths to the Deepwater Horizon spill. On 12 April 2016, a research team reported that 88% of about 360 baby or stillborn dolphins in the spill area had abnormal or under-developed lungs, compared to 15% in other areas, published in Diseases of Aquatic Organisms. By June 2010, 143 spill-exposure cases were reported to the Louisiana Department of Health and Hospitals, with 108 involving cleanup workers and 35 reported by residents; chemicals from oil and dispersants are believed to be the cause, with dispersants making oil more toxic. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services established the GuLF Study in June 2010, run by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, to last at least five years. Mike Robicheux described the situation as "the biggest public health crisis from a chemical poisoning in the history of this country." Environmental scientist Wilma Subra found volatile organic compounds in the blood of BP cleanup workers and residents in Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida at 5 to 10 times the 95th percentile, indicating exposure. Riki Ott, a marine toxicologist with Exxon Valdez experience, advised families to evacuate the Gulf and noted long-term health consequences for Valdez spill workers. Following the hospitalization of seven fishermen in May 2010, BP requested a Health Hazard Evaluation from NIOSH covering offshore cleanup activities and later a second investigation for onshore operations. Tests for chemical exposure in the fishermen were negative; NIOSH concluded the hospitalizations were likely due to heat, fatigue, and terpenes used for deck cleaning. A review of 10 later hospitalizations found heat exposure and dehydration consistently, but could not establish chemical exposure. NIOSH air monitoring found volatile organic compound and PAH concentrations never exceeded permissible levels; a limitation was that some VOCs may have evaporated before testing. NIOSH suggested respiratory symptoms might have been caused by high ozone or reactive aldehydes from photochemical reactions in oil. NIOSH noted that many workers did not use personal protective equipment as instructed and emphasized its importance to prevent transdermal absorption. Heat stress was identified as the most pressing safety concern. Workers reported being denied respirators and threatened with job loss if they used them. OSHA stated cleanup workers received "minimal" exposure to airborne toxins and required BP to provide protective clothing but not respirators. ProPublica reported workers were photographed without protective clothing. An independent Newsweek investigation found BP did not provide the legally required safety manual or safety training or protective gear for Corexit use. A 2012 survey of cleanup workers reported symptoms including eye, nose, and throat irritation; respiratory problems; blood in urine, vomit, and rectal bleeding; seizures; nausea; skin irritation, burning, and lesions; short-term memory loss; liver and kidney damage; central nervous system effects; hypertension; and miscarriages. Dr. James Diaz, writing for the American Journal of Disaster Medicine, noted these symptoms mirrored those after the Exxon Valdez spill and warned of chronic adverse health effects, including cancers, liver and kidney disease, mental health disorders, birth defects, and developmental disorders, especially among sensitive and heavily exposed populations. Two years after the spill, a study by NIOSH found biomarkers matching the spill oil in cleanup workers' bodies. Other studies reported mental health issues, skin problems, breathing issues, coughing, and headaches. At the 2013 Gulf of Mexico Oil Spill & Ecosystem Science Conference, findings included a "significant percentage" of Gulf residents reporting anxiety, depression, and PTSD, with studies showing former cleanup workers carry biomarkers of many oil chemicals. A study of children in Louisiana and Florida living less than 10 miles from the coast found over a third of parents reported physical or mental health symptoms in their children, including bleeding ears, nose bleeds, and early menstruation. A cohort study of nearly 2,200 Louisiana women found high physical/environmental exposure was significantly associated with 13 physical health symptoms, with strongest links to burning in nose, throat, or lungs; sore throat; dizziness; and wheezing. Women with high economic disruption due to the spill were more likely to report wheezing, headaches, watery and burning itchy eyes, and a stuffy, itchy, runny nose. The spill had a major economic impact on BP and Gulf Coast sectors such as offshore drilling, fishing, and tourism. Estimates of lost tourism dollars projected up to $22.7 billion through 2013, with Louisiana losing $32 million in visitor spending by end of 2010 and $153 million by 2013. The Gulf commercial fishing industry lost $247 million due to post-spill closures, and one study projects overall fisheries losses of $8.7 billion by 2020 with a potential loss of 22,000 jobs. BP's expenditures included spill response, containment, relief well drilling, grants, claims, and federal fines and penalties. Due to market value loss, BP dropped from second to fourth largest among U.S. oil companies by 2013. During the crisis, BP gas stations in the U.S. reported sales drops of 10 to 40% due to public backlash. Louisiana officials expressed concern that the offshore drilling moratorium imposed after the spill would harm coastal economies, as the oil industry directly or indirectly employs about 318,000 residents (17% of all state jobs). NOAA closed 86,985 sq mi (225,290 km²), or about 36% of federal Gulf waters, for commercial fishing, causing a $2.5 billion cost to the fishing industry. The U.S. Travel Association estimated the spill's economic impact on Gulf tourism over three years could exceed $23 billion in a region supporting over 400,000 travel jobs generating $34 billion annually. On 30 April 2010, President Barack Obama ordered a halt to new offshore drilling leases and authorized an investigation of 29 oil rigs to determine the cause. A six-month offshore drilling moratorium (below 500 ft or 150 m) was later enforced by the U.S. Department of the Interior, suspending work on 33 rigs, and a group of affected companies formed the Back to Work Coalition. On 22 June, a U.S. federal judge issued a ruling on the matter.

In the Gulf of Mexico, the Deepwater Horizon oil spill caused $2.5 billion in losses for the commercial fishing industry. The U.S. Travel Association estimated that the economic impact on tourism across the Gulf Coast over a three-year period could exceed $23 billion, in a region supporting over 400,000 travel industry jobs that generate $34 billion in annual revenue. On 30 April 2010, President Barack Obama ordered a halt to new offshore drilling leases and authorized an investigation of 29 oil rigs to determine the cause of the disaster. A six-month moratorium on offshore drilling below 500 ft (150 m) of water was enforced by the U.S. Department of the Interior, suspending work on 33 rigs, and a group of affected companies formed the Back to Work Coalition. On 22 June, a U.S. federal judge, Martin Leach-Cross Feldman of the Eastern District of Louisiana, ruled in Hornbeck Offshore Services LLC v. Salazar that the moratorium was too broad, arbitrary, and inadequately justified, and the ban was lifted in October 2010. Prior to the spill, on 31 March 2010, Obama ended a ban on oil and gas drilling along most of the East Coast and northern Alaska to support an energy and climate bill and reduce foreign oil and gas imports. On 28 April 2010, Canada’s National Energy Board issued a letter to oil companies asking them to explain their opposition to safety rules requiring same-season relief wells. On 3 May, California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger withdrew support for expanded offshore drilling in California. On 8 July, Florida Governor Charlie Crist called for a special session to draft a constitutional amendment banning offshore drilling in state waters, which the legislature rejected on 20 July. In October 2011, the U.S. Department of the Interior’s Minerals Management Service was dissolved due to poor oversight, replaced by three new agencies: the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, and the Office of Natural Resources Revenue. In March 2014, BP was allowed to bid for oil and gas leases again. On 30 April, President Obama sent the Secretaries of Interior and Homeland Security, the EPA Administrator, and NOAA to the Gulf Coast to assess the disaster. In his 15 June speech, Obama stated, "This oil spill is the worst environmental disaster America has ever faced... We will fight this spill with everything we've got for as long as it takes. We will make BP pay for the damage their company has caused. And we will do whatever's necessary to help the Gulf Coast and its people recover from this tragedy." Interior Secretary Ken Salazar said, "Our job basically is to keep the boot on the neck of British Petroleum." Some observers suggested the Obama administration was overly aggressive, with some BP investors viewing it as an attempt to deflect criticism of Obama’s crisis management. Rand Paul accused Obama of being anti-business and "un-American." Public opinion polls in the U.S. were generally critical of how President Obama and the federal government handled the disaster and were extremely critical of BP’s response. Across the U.S., thousands participated in dozens of protests at BP gas stations and other locations, reducing sales at some stations by 10% to 40%. An academic study noted that the severity of disruption significantly influenced the social construction of the event, as policy actors were ill-equipped to manage the challenges at all levels. The petroleum industry claimed disasters are infrequent and that this spill was an isolated incident, rejecting claims of lost industry credibility. The American Petroleum Institute (API) stated that offshore drilling is important for job creation and economic growth. CEOs from the top five oil companies agreed to improve safety, and API announced the creation of an offshore safety institute separate from its lobbying operations. The Organization for International Investment warned that heated rhetoric could damage British companies’ reputations in the U.S. and spark U.S. protectionism affecting government contracts, political donations, and lobbying. In July 2010, President Obama issued an executive order citing the Deepwater Horizon spill, adopting recommendations from the Interagency Ocean Policy Task Force and establishing the National Ocean Council, which brought together federal committees and departments on ocean issues to work with a new conservation and resource management committee. In June 2018, President Donald Trump revoked this executive order to roll back bureaucracy and benefit "ocean industries that employ millions of Americans." In the UK, there was anger at U.S. media for using the term "British Petroleum," which was discontinued in 1998 when British Petroleum merged with Amoco to form BP Amoco. It was claimed the U.S. was "dumping" blame on the British public, with calls for British Prime Minister David Cameron to protect British interests. British pension fund managers, who hold large BP shares and rely on its dividends, accepted that while BP had to pay compensation, the cost to its market value from Obama’s criticism outweighed direct clean-up costs. Initially, BP downplayed the incident; CEO Tony Hayward called the oil and dispersant amounts "relatively tiny" compared to the "very big ocean." Later, he faced criticism when he said the spill disrupted Gulf Coast residents and added, "You know, I'd like my life back." BP’s chief operating officer Doug Suttles contradicted claims of an underwater plume, stating, "It may be down to how you define what a plume is here… The oil that has been found is in very minute quantities." In June 2010, BP launched a PR campaign and successfully bid for search terms related to the spill on Google and other search engines so that the first sponsored result linked to its website. On 26 July 2010, CEO Tony Hayward was to resign and was replaced by Bob Dudley, an American citizen who previously worked for Amoco. Hayward became a highly controversial public figure; in May 2013, he was honored as a "distinguished leader" by the University of Birmingham, but the award ceremony was repeatedly interrupted by jeers and walk-outs and protests from People & Planet members. In July 2013, Hayward received an honorary degree from Robert Gordon University, which Friends of the Earth Scotland described as a "sick joke" and "a very serious error of judgement," with the student body president expressing disappointment. The U.S. government rejected offers of cleanup help from Canada, Croatia, France, Germany, Ireland, Mexico, the Netherlands, Norway, Romania, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United Nations. The U.S. State Department listed 70 assistance offers from 23 countries, all initially declined, but eight were later accepted. The U.S. Coast Guard actively requested skimming boats and equipment from several countries. The U.S. Deepwater Horizon investigation included several investigations and commissions, including reports by: the Republic of the Marshall Islands Maritime Administrator, BP’s internal investigation, a U.S. Coast Guard and Minerals Management Service investigation launched on 22 April 2010, a request from the U.S. administration on 11 May for the National Academy of Engineering to conduct an independent technical investigation, and the establishment on 22 May of the National Commission on the BP Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill and Offshore Drilling to "consider the root causes of the disaster and offer options on safety and environmental precautions." The U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder announced an investigation on 1 June 2010. The House Committee on Energy and Commerce conducted hearings, including those of Tony Hayward and heads of Anadarko and Mitsui’s exploration unit. According to the congressional investigation, the rig’s blowout preventer, built by Cameron International Corporation, had a hydraulic leak and a failed battery, and therefore failed. On 8 September 2010, BP released a 193-page report on its website placing some blame on BP, Halliburton, and Transocean. The report found that on 20 April 2010, managers misread pressure data and approved replacing drilling fluid with seawater, which was not heavy enough to prevent gas from igniting, causing the explosion. BP, Transocean, and Halliburton were each partly to blame. Responding, Transocean and Halliburton placed all blame on BP. On 9 November 2010, the Oil Spill Commission reported that there had been "a rush to completion" and criticized poor management decisions, stating, "There was not a culture of safety on that rig." The National Commission on the BP Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill and Offshore Drilling released a final report on 5 January 2011. The panel found that BP, Halliburton, and Transocean attempted to work more cheaply, which helped trigger the explosion and subsequent leakage. The report stated that "whether purposeful or not, many of the decisions that BP, Halliburton, and Transocean made that increased the risk of the Macondo blowout clearly saved those companies significant time (and money)." BP stated that "even prior to the conclusion of the commission's investigation, BP instituted significant changes designed to further strengthen safety and risk management." Transocean blamed BP for making the decisions before the explosion and government officials for permitting them. Halliburton stated it acted only upon BP’s orders when injecting cement into the well and criticized BP for failing to run a cement bond log test. The report accused BP of nine faults, including not using a diagnostic tool to test cement strength, ignoring a failed pressure test, and not plugging the pipe with cement. The report concluded that "notwithstanding these inherent risks, the accident of April 20 was avoidable" and that "it resulted from clear mistakes made in the first instance by BP, Halliburton and Transocean, and by government officials who, relying too much on industry's assertions of the safety of their operations, failed to create and apply a program of regulatory oversight that would have properly minimized the risk of deepwater drilling." The panel also noted that government regulators lacked sufficient knowledge or authority to notice cost-cutting decisions. On 23 March 2011, BOEMRE (former MMS) and the U.S. Coast Guard published a forensic examination report on the blowout preventer by Det Norske Veritas, concluding that the primary cause of failure was that the blind shear rams failed to fully close and seal due to a portion of drill pipe buckling between the shearing blocks. A U.S. government report issued in September 2011 stated that BP is ultimately responsible for the spill, with Halliburton and Transocean sharing some blame. The report identified the main cause as a defective cement job, and stated that Halliburton, BP, and Transocean were responsible in different ways. It noted that although the events leading to the sinking of Deepwater Horizon were set in motion by the failure to prevent a well blowout, the investigation revealed numerous systems deficiencies and acts and omissions by Transocean and its crew that adversely impacted the ability to prevent or limit the disaster. A central cause of the blowout was the failure of a cement barrier allowing hydrocarbons to flow up the wellbore, through the riser, and onto the rig, resulting in the blowout. The loss of life and subsequent pollution of the Gulf of Mexico resulted from poor risk management, last-minute changes to plans, failure to observe and respond to critical indicators, inadequate well control response, and insufficient emergency bridge response training by companies and individuals responsible for drilling at the Macondo well and for the operation of the drilling platform. On 16 June 2010, after BP executives met with President Obama, BP announced and established the Gulf Coast Claims Facility (GCCF), a $20 billion fund to settle claims from the Deepwater Horizon spill, covering natural resource damages, state and local response costs, and individual compensation, but not fines or penalties. Prior to the GCCF, emergency compensation was paid by BP from an initial facility. The GCCF was administered by attorney Kenneth Feinberg and began accepting claims on 23 August 2010. On 8 March 2012, after BP and a team of plaintiffs' attorneys agreed to a class-action settlement, a court-supervised administrator, Patrick Juneau, took over administration. Over one million claims from 220,000 individual and business claimants were processed, and more than $6.2 billion was paid out, with 97% of payments going to claimants in the Gulf States. In June 2012, the GCCF settlement was replaced by a court-supervised settlement program, during which an additional $404 million in claims were paid. The GCCF and Feinberg were criticized for the amount and speed of payments and a lack of transparency. An independent audit of the GCCF, approved by the Senate on 21 October 2011, found that 7,300 claimants were wrongly denied or underpaid, resulting in about $64 million in additional payments. The Mississippi Center for Justice provided pro bono assistance to 10,000 people to help them navigate the claims process. In a New York Times opinion piece, Stephen Teague, staff attorney at the Mississippi Center for Justice, argued that BP had become "increasingly brazen" in "stonewalling payments," noting that tens of thousands of Gulf residents still had not been fully compensated, and many were struggling financially, especially low-wage workers in fishing and service industries seeking compensation for lost wages and jobs for three years. In July 2013, BP filed a motion in court to freeze payments on tens of thousands of claims, arguing that a staff attorney from the Deepwater Horizon Court-Supervised Settlement Program had improperly profited from claims filed by a New Orleans law firm. The attorney is said to have received portions of settlement claims for clients he referred to the firm. Federal Judge Barbier refused to halt the settlement program, stating he had not seen evidence of widespread fraud and that he was "offended by what he saw as attempts to smear the lawyer administering the claims." By 26 May 2010, over 130 lawsuits had been filed against one or more of BP, Transocean, Cameron International Corporation, or Halliburton Energy Services, though observers expected these to be combined into one multidistrict litigation. On 21 April 2011, BP issued $40 billion in lawsuits against rig owner Transocean, cementer Halliburton, and blowout preventer manufacturer Cameron, alleging failed safety systems and irresponsible contractor behavior, including claims that Halliburton failed to properly use modeling software to analyze safe drilling conditions. The firms denied the allegations. On 2 March 2012, BP and plaintiffs agreed to settle roughly 100,000 claims filed by individuals and businesses affected by the spill.

By 26 May 2010, over 130 lawsuits had been filed against BP, Transocean, Cameron International Corporation, or Halliburton Energy Services relating to the spill, with observers expecting these to be consolidated into one multidistrict litigation. On 21 April 2011, BP filed $40 billion in lawsuits against Transocean, Halliburton, and Cameron, alleging failed safety systems and irresponsible contractor behavior, including that Halliburton improperly used modeling software to assess safe drilling conditions; the firms denied the claims. On 2 March 2012, BP and plaintiffs agreed to settle roughly 100,000 claims involving individuals and businesses affected by the spill. On 13 August 2012, BP requested U.S. District Judge Carl Barbier to approve the settlement, asserting its actions did not constitute gross negligence or willful misconduct. On 13 January 2013, Judge Barbier approved a medical-benefits portion of BP’s proposed $7.8 billion partial settlement, covering individuals who lived for at least 60 days along oil-impacted shores or participated in cleanup and can document specific health conditions caused by oil or dispersants, as well as those injured during cleanup. BP also committed $105 million over five years for a Gulf Coast health outreach program and medical exams. A plaintiff group stated the deal had no specific cap, and BP maintained $9.5 billion in assets set aside in a trust to pay claims, with the settlement not increasing the $37.2 billion originally budgeted for spill-related expenses; BP initially expected to spend $7.8 billion, raising its projection to $9.2 billion by October 2013, citing it could be "significantly higher." On 31 August 2012, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed papers in federal court in New Orleans blaming BP for the Gulf oil spill, describing it as an example of "gross negligence and willful misconduct," calling some of BP’s arguments "plainly misleading" and stating the court should disregard BP’s claim that the Gulf region was "undergoing a robust recovery"; BP rejected the charges, asserting it was not grossly negligent and looking forward to presenting evidence at trial in January. The DOJ also charged Transocean, the rig owner and operator, with gross negligence. On 14 November 2012, BP and the DOJ reached a settlement: BP paid $4.5 billion in fines and other payments, the largest of its kind in U.S. history, and was temporarily banned from new federal contracts due to "lack of business integrity"; the plea was accepted by Judge Sarah Vance on 31 January 2013. The settlement included $2.394 billion to the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, $1.15 billion to the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, $350 million to the National Academy of Sciences for oil spill prevention and response research, $100 million to the North America Wetland Conservation Fund, $6 million to General Treasury, and $525 million to the Securities and Exchange Commission. Oil sector analysts at Canaccord Genuity noted the settlement would only be a partial resolution of the many claims against BP. On 3 January 2013, the DOJ announced that Transocean Deepwater Inc. agreed to plead guilty to violating the Clean Water Act and pay a total of $1.4 billion in civil and criminal fines and penalties: $800 million to the Gulf Coast restoration Trust Fund, $300 million to the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, $150 million to the National Wild Turkey Federation, and $150 million to the National Academy of Sciences; MOEX Offshore 2007 agreed to pay $45 million to the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, $25 million to five Gulf states, and $20 million to supplemental environmental projects. On 25 July 2013, Halliburton pleaded guilty to destroying critical evidence after the spill and agreed to pay the maximum allowable fine of $200,000 and serve three years of probation. In January 2014, a panel of the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected BP’s effort to limit payments to what it called "fictitious" and "absurd" claims in the settlement fund, ruling that BP had not explained how the court could identify claimants without cognizable injury and calling BP’s position "nonsensical"; the Supreme Court later refused to hear BP’s appeal after victims, claimants, and Gulf coast chambers of commerce objected to BP’s attempt to renege on the settlement. In September 2014, Halliburton settled a large percentage of legal claims against it by paying $1.1 billion into a trust in three installments over two years. BP and its partners—Transocean and Halliburton—went on trial on 25 February 2013 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana in New Orleans to determine payouts and fines under the Clean Water Act and the Natural Resources Damage Assessment, with plaintiffs including the U.S. Justice Department, Gulf states, and private individuals; tens of billions of dollars in liability and fines were at stake. A finding of gross negligence would result in a four-fold increase in BP’s Clean Water Act fines and liability for punitive damages in private claims. The trial’s first phase assessed liability and whether BP, Transocean, Halliburton, and others acted with gross negligence and willful misconduct; the second phase in September 2013 focused on the oil flow rate, and the third phase in 2014 on damages. Plaintiffs’ lawyers attributed the explosion to mishandling of a rig safety test, inadequate staff training, poor equipment maintenance, and substandard cement. The Wall Street Journal reported the U.S. government and Gulf Coast states had prepared a $16 billion settlement offer to BP, though it was unclear if it was officially proposed or accepted. On 4 September 2014, U.S. District Judge Carl Barbier ruled BP guilty of gross negligence and willful misconduct, describing its actions as "reckless," and found Transocean’s and Halliburton’s actions to be "negligent." He assigned 67% of the blame to BP, 30% to Transocean, and 3% to Halliburton. Fines would be proportioned to the degree of negligence, based on the number of barrels spilled, with Clean Water Act fines potentially up to $4,300 per barrel at the judge’s discretion. The number of barrels spilled was disputed: BP argued 2.5 million barrels over 87 days, while the court asserted 4.2 million barrels. BP strongly disagreed with the ruling and filed an immediate appeal. Barbier ruled BP acted with "conscious disregard of known risks," rejected BP’s assertion of equal responsibility among parties, and stated BP employees took risks leading to the largest environmental disaster in U.S. history, with key decisions driven by a desire to save time and money rather than ensuring well security. BP strongly disputed the ruling and filed an immediate appeal. On 2 July 2015, BP, the U.S. Justice Department, and five Gulf states announced a record $18.7 billion settlement. To date, BP’s total costs for clean-up, environmental and economic damages, and penalties have reached $54 billion. In addition to private lawsuits and civil actions, the federal government charged multiple companies and five individuals with federal crimes. In the November 2012 resolution of federal charges against BP, the company pleaded guilty to 11 felony counts related to the deaths of 11 workers and paid a $4 billion fine; Transocean pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor as part of its $1.4 billion fine. In April 2012, the DOJ filed the first criminal charge against Kurt Mix, a BP engineer, for obstructing justice by deleting messages showing BP knew the flow rate was three times higher than claimed and that the "Top Kill" method was unlikely to succeed; three more BP employees were charged in November 2012: site managers Donald Vidrine and Robert Kaluza were charged with manslaughter for negligent supervision of safety tests and failure to alert onshore engineers of drilling problems, and David Rainey, BP’s former vice-president for Gulf exploration, was charged with obstructing Congress by misrepresenting the oil flow rate; Anthony Badalamenti, a Halliburton manager, was charged with instructing two employees to delete data related to Halliburton’s cementing job. None of the individual charges resulted in prison time, and no upper-level executives were charged. Anthony Badalamenti was sentenced to one year probation, Donald Vidrine paid a $50,000 fine and received 10 months probation, Kurt Mix received six months’ probation, and David Rainey and Robert Kaluza were acquitted.
